title: The Destruction of the Scottish Canon
author: Alec Thompson
summary: Thompson reconstructs how Scotland dismantled a secondary curriculum once ranked among the world's best, using interviews with retired civil servants and a century of past exam papers. He places the Curriculum for Excellence of 2011 inside a wider pattern, since Sweden, France, Germany, Japan and England all replaced content with general analysis and synthesis tasks between 1990 and 2010, driven variously by egalitarian and free-market motives that converged on the same logic. The Scottish story turns on institutional capture, as a vocational qualifications body absorbed the examination board in what former members called a hostile takeover, and on a 2007 OECD report, influenced by Bourdieu, that diagnosed the system's problem as being too academic. Thompson then asks whether the reforms delivered: scores have fallen almost continuously, the apparent narrowing of the socioeconomic gap came from higher-status pupils falling faster, and by 2022 even that disappeared. His theoretical objection is that general thinking skills of the kind the model assumes do not meaningfully exist, since expertise is domain-specific and text analysis depends on prior knowledge of the subject matter. He closes by noting the countries that kept or restored knowledge, and by quoting Lindsay Paterson's judgment that the old tradition now survives only as a set of documents.
points: Documents that the same knowledge-to-skills substitution was adopted across six countries between 1990 and 2010 from opposite political motives, which suggests the reform travelled as an assumption rather than a finding.
Traces the Scottish mechanism to the merger in which a vocational qualifications body absorbed the examination board, and to a 2007 OECD report faulting the system for an excessive academic culture.
Shows the equity rationale failed on its own terms, since the 2012 to 2018 narrowing came from high-status scores falling faster and vanished entirely by 2022.
Argues the model rests on general thinking skills that expertise research does not support, since analysing a text depends mainly on prior knowledge of its subject matter.
Lists the countries that kept knowledge or returned to it, including Japan, Poland, Germany and England after 2014, against Scotland's refusal to revisit the reform.
quotes: In 2011, Scotland destroyed its secondary school curriculum, once ranked among the best in the world. It was not the first country to do so.
All of the reforms had the same logic: Remove facts, content, and structure, and replace them with general analysis and synthesis tasks.

The loss of these traditions might have been justifiable had they achieved the goals of the reformers. In each country, however, the reforms have been accompanied by sharp declines in reading, writing, and mathematics competencies.

The report — heavily influenced by the French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu — found Scotland had unacceptable levels of educational inequality and claimed it was produced by overemphasis on structured knowledge in the place of a more holistic skills-based approach.
The modest reduction in socioeconomic educational inequality between 2012 and 2018 was driven primarily by the high-status students’ scores falling faster than their low-status peers.
Consider the theoretical assumption at the heart of modern skills-based pedagogy: “general thinking skills.” Expertise studies suggest no such skill with any meaningful effect exists.

Some countries met the postwar challenge by adapting their traditional, knowledge-rich curricula. Singapore, China, Estonia, and Ireland retained knowledge in their curriculum; equally, they remain some of the top performing countries according to the OECD.
The Tradition’s destruction is a tragedy. Knowledge enriches life and cannot be acquired outside a course of disciplined study.
